newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan banks look to reduce overseas credit risks.
newsitem.headline: Japan banks look to reduce overseas credit risks.

text.p: Major Japanese commercial banks have either started or are considering engaging in so-called credit derivatives contracts to hedge against the risk of loan defaults in developing countries.

Sanwa Bank Ltd has clinched several credit risk contracts with foreign investors this year, to hedge against the risk of default on its loans to Asian and Latin American countries, the bank's official in charge of international finance told Reuters.
Other major banks, such as Fuji Bank Ltd, are also considering credit derivatives as a way to reduce their exposure to risks from overseas lending.
Under a credit derivatives contract, the buyer, or the taker of the risk, receives a premium from the seller in return for taking up the risk that the borrower might default on the loan.
If a default does occur, the buyer of the risk must either buy that non-performing asset entirely from the seller, or pay a sum that will cover the depreciation of that asset.
"Our ability to lend overseas is limited by credit quotas set for each country. However, through the use of credit derivatives, we could create more room to lend," the Sanwa official said.
Each deal normally lasts one to three years, according to the official.
"As a seller of credit risks, we would like to do longer deals, but risk-takers naturally are hesitant to carry risks for the long term," he said.
In the future, the bank hopes to find investors willing to shoulder some of the risks posed by its loans to places such as eastern Europe, the official added.
The credit derivatives market has grown rapidly in the United States and Europe since major U.S. commercial banks and investment banks began conducting deals in the early 1990s.
Market sources say the size of the market is now worth about $50 billion worldwide. No official figure is available.

"We would like to do more deals by the end of this fiscal year (ending in March 1997), but as each deal normally takes two to three months to sign, it won't be that easy to increase deals rapidly," the Sanwa official said.
An official at Fuji Bank said the bank was also considering using credit derivatives to reduce its loan exposure in developing countries.

"There may be many areas where credit derivatives could be applied, but at this stage, the strongest need lies in hedging overseas credit risks. In the future, however, we may be able to use them in other areas as well," he said.
An official at another major city bank, who declined to be named, said his bank was already conducting credit derivative deals on behalf of clients who want to reduce their exposure.
"As for using credit derivatives as an end-user, that is for our own purposes, we are just studying the possibility at this stage," he said.
On average, a credit derivatives deal is worth about $50 million to $100 million, he said.
As for the possibility of credit derivatives being used in Japan's domestic market in the future, however, the official was pessimistic.

"Unlike in the U.S., a fair pricing of credit risk is difficult in Japan, as lending rates here do not necessarily reflect borrowers' credit ratings. Therefore, I personally do not think a credit derivatives market would be established in Japan," he said.
